cards.headline: Vero Beach group collects emergency supplies for Venezuela earthquake victims through Saturday
cards.teaser: Latinas Nexus Network in Vero Beach is collecting donations for communities devastated by a massive earthquake in Venezuela.
cards.body:
Latinas Nexus Network in Vero Beach is hosting a Venezuela Earthquake Relief Drive to collect essential supplies for communities devastated by a 7.5 magnitude earthquake. The drive is being organized by founders Lourana Navarro and Juliana Marino, along with Heidi Ramirez. Navarro, who was born in Venezuela, said her family in Caracas is safe, but surrounding communities have lost everything. She said the scale of destruction will take years to address. The organizers are working with Global Empowerment Mission to ship collected supplies to Venezuela, with 100% of donations directed through verified humanitarian relief efforts.

Donations can be dropped off at 684 Old Dixie Hwy, Vero Beach through Saturday, June 27, 2026, from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. The organization is collecting powder Gatorade, non-perishable food, baby formula and baby food, diapers in all sizes, baby wipes, feminine hygiene products, soap, shampoo, toothbrushes and toothpaste, rain boots, toilet paper, blankets, sleeping bags, flashlights and batteries, heavy duty garbage bags, first aid kits, bandages and gauze, hand sanitizer, cleaning supplies, face masks, nitrile medical gloves, and plastic bins with lids. The drive is open to everyone, not just the local Hispanic community. To contact organizers, call Lourana Navarro at (954) 205-0700, Juliana Marino at (772) 913-0805, or Heidi Ramirez at (772) 213-2747.

cards.headline: Missing diver found dead on ocean floor near Fort Pierce Inlet
cards.teaser: A missing diver was found dead on the ocean floor approximately 6 to 7 miles north-northeast of the Fort Pierce Inlet on Friday afternoon.
cards.body:
The St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office is investigating after a missing diver was found dead on the ocean floor approximately 6 to 7 miles north-northeast of the Fort Pierce Inlet. The U.S. Coast Guard Station Fort Pierce received a Mayday call over VHF Channel 16 at approximately 11:30 a.m. Friday regarding the missing diver. Following the distress call, the Coast Guard notified the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission, which immediately deployed 4 vessels to assist in the search. The St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office Marine Unit, which had independently monitored the Mayday call, was already en route to assist.

A group of civilian boaters who were friends of the missing diver departed the Fort Pierce Inlet at approximately 1 p.m., with aerial support provided by both the Coast Guard and FWC. Responding units made contact with the vessel involved nearly due east of Avalon State Park. At approximately 4:10 p.m., civilian divers entered the water and located the missing diver at the bottom of the ocean in approximately 55 feet of water. The diver was recovered and pronounced deceased. The deceased was transported to Coast Guard Station Fort Pierce. The St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office Criminal Investigations Division is conducting the ongoing investigation into the circumstances surrounding the incident.

cards.headline: Orbeez toy gun prank in Port St. Lucie leads to 2 arrests after man holds teens at gunpoint
cards.teaser: A 49-year-old man and a 15-year-old were arrested Wednesday evening after an Orbeez prank escalated into an armed confrontation near SW Morelia Lane and SW Acap.
cards.body:
A 49-year-old man and a 15-year-old were arrested Wednesday evening after an Orbeez prank escalated into an armed confrontation near SW Morelia Lane and SW Acapulco Terrace in Port St. Lucie. Gregory Allen Davis and his fiancée called 911 to report being shot at while driving, believing they had been hit by a BB or pellet gun. The two began following the vehicle as Port St. Lucie police deployed their first responder drone. While his fiancée remained on the phone with the dispatcher, Davis exited his vehicle and shouted at the teens to exit theirs, an encounter captured by a witness. Armed with a 9mm handgun, Davis ordered the teens to the ground at gunpoint. Officers arrived moments later and discovered an Orbeez toy gun had been used in the incident.

Police interviewed three teens who claimed they thought the other vehicle belonged to a friend and shot at it with the Orbeez gun as part of a game. According to PSLPD, Davis had multiple opportunities to safely disengage while officers were actively responding. Davis was charged with aggravated assault with a deadly weapon without intent to kill and false imprisonment of a child to commit aggravated abuse. A 15-year-old was charged with shooting or throwing a missile at or into an occupied vehicle. PSLPD stated the incident serves as a reminder that pranks involving Orbeez guns, airsoft guns, BB guns, or other toy firearms are not harmless and can create fear, provoke dangerous reactions, and result in criminal charges.

cards.headline: Florida farm labor cases mirror Italy's migrant worker exploitation system
cards.body:
Federal prosecutors in Tampa and across Florida have brought forced labor cases against farm contractors that operate using methods similar to criminal systems documented in Italy. The Italian case involved four migrant workers who were burned alive in a van in Calabria after demanding unpaid wages. Experts describe this type of exploitation as the gangmaster economy, where criminal intermediaries control workers through debt, threats and isolation. In Italy, this system has a specific name: caporalato. The caporale recruits workers, controls transportation, decides pay rates and determines where workers sleep and whether they can leave.

The Italian system has adapted to changing migration patterns. For decades, caporalato was associated with traditional Italian organized crime groups. But a division of labor has emerged where foreign criminal networks now handle direct control of workers because they better understand migrant vulnerabilities. Many workers now come from Afghanistan, Pakistan, Syria and other distant countries. These workers often arrive with travel debts, do not speak Italian, lack local connections and depend entirely on intermediaries for work, transportation and housing. Criminal networks exploit this dependence, even threatening relatives in workers' home countries to enforce compliance.

In Florida, Alexander Villatoro Moreno, known as Quichi, was sentenced to 70 months in prison on June 9 in federal court in Tampa after pleading guilty to a RICO conspiracy. He and co-defendants operated Los Villatoros Harvesting, which brought Mexican workers to the United States on H-2A agricultural visas. Prosecutors said workers were promised fair wages and good conditions but faced excessive recruitment fees and debt upon arrival. They were kept in crowded housing, isolated from outsiders, verbally humiliated and threatened with arrest or deportation. The conspirators also threatened to harm workers' family members in Mexico. A second case involved Martha Zeferino Jose, her partner and her son, charged in a 35-count indictment in February involving Las Princesas Corp. According to prosecutors, the company recruited Mexican H-2A workers for farms and nurseries in Virginia, North Carolina and Florida while confiscating documents, imposing debts, providing degrading housing and threatening deportation.

The H-2A program is a legal guest worker system that many employers use lawfully. However, a worker arriving with papers remains vulnerable. They may depend on a single employer for their job, one contractor for transportation and one document for their legal status. If that chain turns criminal, the legal route becomes part of the trap. Federal prosecutors have used forced labor and racketeering laws against farm contractors, but convictions often come years after workers have suffered. By that time, the system has already inflicted damage. Italy announced increased farm inspections after the Calabria killings, but the question of timing remains difficult.

hero.headline: Florida governor signs new property tax restrictions as Amendment 3 battle heats up
hero.teaser: Gov. Ron DeSantis signed new laws tightening how cities and counties can raise property-tax revenue while a November constitutional amendment threatens further budget cuts for local governments.
hero.body:
Governor DeSantis has signed legislation that restricts how cities, counties and special districts can increase property tax revenue. The new laws require local governments to stay closer to the rollback rate, which is designed to generate roughly the same tax revenue as the previous year. Any attempt to exceed this rate now requires a larger voter approval threshold. Florida Chief Financial Officer Blaise Ingoglia emphasized the need for government at all levels to pursue spending cuts rather than revenue increases.

Those backing the new restrictions argue they protect taxpayers by preventing local government budgets from expanding too quickly as property values climb. However, local officials have expressed serious concerns. They warn that these new laws, combined with the proposed constitutional amendment on the November ballot, could create significant budget shortfalls for cities and counties. The combination of restrictions may force difficult choices about essential services and spending priorities.

Amendment 3, scheduled to appear on voters' ballots in November, would expand homestead property tax exemptions on non-school taxes. The exemption would increase to $150,000 in 2027 and then rise to $250,000 in 2028. Supporters contend the amendment would provide meaningful financial relief to homeowners facing rising property values. Critics counter that while some property owners would save money, the revenue losses could trigger service reductions, higher fees, or increased taxes elsewhere to compensate for lost income.

The property tax debate has intensified with the launch of a new outside campaign urging voters to reject Amendment 3. This campaign adds another dimension to what is expected to become one of Florida's most closely watched ballot measures this election cycle. The clash between those seeking property tax relief and those concerned about government funding reflects a broader disagreement over how to balance homeowner protection with maintaining local services.

cards.headline: Everglades environmental groups and Miccosukee Tribe say fight continues after Alligator Alcatraz closure
cards.teaser: Trailers are rolling out of the immigration detention center known as Alligator Alcatraz, but environmental advocates say the closure alone does not undo harm to the Everglades ecosystem.
cards.body:
Trailers are rolling out of the remote immigration detention center in the Everglades known as Alligator Alcatraz, but environmental advocates and members of the Miccosukee Tribe say the fight over the land is far from over. A group gathered at the entrance Friday morning as the facility that once held undocumented immigrants is being dismantled piece by piece. Betty Osceola of the Miccosukee Tribe said the closure alone does not undo the harm to one of the most sensitive ecosystems in the country. "It's not over for me until all that infrastructure comes out," Osceola said. Environmental advocates say high-intensity lighting, diesel generators, heavy paving and continuous traffic may have damaged critical habitat for endangered Florida panthers and other wildlife. Eve Samples, executive director of Friends of the Everglades, called the facility an obscene waste of taxpayer dollars, to the tune of about a billion dollars. The group has a pending federal lawsuit against the facility.

A recent proposal from Miami-Dade County's mayor would transfer the roughly 25,000-acre space to the National Park Service for conservation. However, Osceola said she does not trust government agencies to protect the land. She said the Miccosukee people are the rightful stewards of the landscape, noting that her family has been foraging for food and living on this land. Elise Bennett of the Center for Biological Diversity said the harm to the Everglades has not been undone by the announcement of closure.

cards.headline: Republican governor's race intensifies with no debate scheduled before August 18 primary
cards.teaser: U.S. Rep. Byron Donalds remains the only Republican candidate meeting the party's debate criteria while rivals Paul Renner, Lt. Jay Collins and James Fishback continue calling for a head-to-head contest.
cards.body:
With Florida's Aug. 18 primary approaching, the Republican race for governor intensified this week without a debate stage materializing. U.S. Rep. Byron Donalds remains the only Republican candidate meeting the party's debate criteria, while rivals Paul Renner, Lt. Jay Collins and James Fishback continue arguing voters deserve a head-to-head contest before ballots are cast. Renner criticized the debate process in a recent interview, suggesting internal party politics are protecting the frontrunner. Donalds rebuffed the calls during a Florida Chamber press conference announcing their endorsement, calling the governor's race a job interview. "If I'm applying for a job, it's not my responsibility to help my competitor get a job interview," Donalds said.

The candidates are accelerating efforts elsewhere. Collins announced a "multi-million dollar statewide" advertising blitz, while Donalds is planning a $20 million statewide ad buy through the primary. Fishback named former South Florida police officer Sean Lozano as his running mate and deputy campaign manager. At the Tallahassee announcement, Lozano said they will not politely manage Florida's decline but will stop it. No debate has materialized even from local news outlets as the race moves quickly forward.

cards.headline: John Morgan's new political party named Common Ground Party
cards.teaser: Orlando attorney John Morgan announced his new political party will be called the Common Ground Party with members known as Grounders after a $100,000 naming contest.
cards.body:
Orlando attorney John Morgan announced this week that his new political party will be called the Common Ground Party, with members known as "Grounders." The name was selected from a $100,000 contest, with the prize money to be shared among more than 250 people who suggested "Common Ground Party." Morgan said he is uncertain whether the effort will succeed, but believes it is worth attempting to undo the gridlock, hate, and meanness that has entered politics on all sides.

Morgan has positioned the party as an option for voters frustrated with both Democrats and Republicans. However, significant questions remain unanswered about the party's platform, whether it can secure ballot access, and whether the Grounders can develop into a legitimate political force or become another short-lived third-party experiment in Florida politics.

cards.headline: Alligator Alcatraz detainees scattered across U.S. as legal battles continue
cards.teaser: Detainees from the closed Everglades immigration facility have been moved to Louisiana, Texas, New Mexico and as far as Tacoma, Washington, creating challenges for families and attorneys.
cards.body:
Immigration attorney Richard Hujber said detainees from the now-closed Alligator Alcatraz facility have been transferred to detention centers across the country, including Louisiana, Texas, New Mexico, and as far as Tacoma, Washington. According to Hujber, these transfers create significant legal challenges because immigration law varies across different circuit courts nationwide. With bond becoming unattainable for some detainees in certain circuits, many are forced to decide whether to continue fighting for residency or asylum or to self-deport. Gov. Ron DeSantis reported that approximately 21,000 people have been deported from the Everglades facility since it opened nearly a year ago.

For some detainees, the facility's closure brought relief. Anna Maria Hernandez's cousin was released just before Alligator Alcatraz shut down and is now under an order of supervision, which allows him to drive, work and live in the U.S. However, Hujber emphasized that the decision to continue fighting immigration cases ultimately rests with the detainees themselves, not their families. The Baker County facility in North Florida remains operational. For many former detainees and their families, uncertainty about the future persists.

cards.headline: Martin County woman sentenced to 29 years for killing cyclist on 10-Cent Bridge
cards.teaser: Elise Elder, 25, was sentenced Friday to just over 29 years in prison for the death of 67-year-old Martin Drummond, who was killed while riding his bike on the 10-Cent Bridge in June 2024.
cards.body:
Elise Elder, 25, was sentenced Friday to just over 29 years in prison for the June 2024 death of 67-year-old Martin Drummond on the 10-Cent Bridge. She received 17 years for fleeing the scene and just over 12 years for DUI manslaughter, to be served consecutively, plus one year probation and a lifetime license revocation. Florida Highway Patrol said Drummond was riding his bike east on A1A toward South Sewall's Point Road in the bike lane at approximately 6:45 a.m. when Elder's 2019 BMW 535I went into the bike lane and rear-ended him. Elder fled the scene and was arrested at her residence. Investigators determined Elder was driving drunk from Daytona Beach and was over the legal limit at the time of her arrest.

Drummond was a well-known Stuart community member, publisher of a local magazine, and known as a mentor and spiritual leader. During sentencing, Elder expressed remorse, stating "I want to be accountable to myself and everyone in this room. I destroyed a family and life of an innocent human being, and I'm so sorry and regretful of that." His widow, Lori Drummond, said she forgives Elder. Daughters Jessica Cornett and Melissa Cooke described the ongoing impact of his death on their family and lives.

hero.headline: Boca Raton homeowner waits on My Safe Florida Home grant despite completed work
hero.teaser: Anne Bendel of West Boca Raton says her application for a My Safe Florida Home grant keeps facing new hurdles even though she completed all required work and paid $8,000 out of pocket.
hero.body:
Anne Bendel says she has done everything required to receive a state grant for home improvements, but the My Safe Florida Home program keeps asking for more documentation. The West Boca Raton homeowner first reached out to WPTV in May after her application stalled due to missing paperwork from her insurance company. Once that issue was resolved, program officials told her in May that her status was complete.

The relief was short-lived. A week after receiving word her application was finished, My Safe Florida Home representatives requested additional documents, specifically a permit of completion for a large impact window. Bendel provided the permit, but then officials raised questions about dates on her paperwork. Her application went back under review, leaving her uncertain whether she will receive any of the grant money she was promised. She paid $8,000 out of pocket for the home improvements and is hoping the state program will help cover those costs.

Bendel describes the process as exhausting, especially because she is working through the application on her phone without a computer or assistance from others. "I did the work, I had it completed, I got the permits, I had the insurance they asked for. Everything is done, but it seems like when everything is done they find some other little task to send you," she said. She expressed frustration that the program continues to request additional items even after officials declared her application complete.

The My Safe Florida Home program offers grants of up to $10,000 to help homeowners across Florida strengthen their homes against storms and qualify for insurance discounts. The initiative has assisted thousands of residents. However, Bendel's experience has shaken her confidence in the program's ability to deliver on its promises. WPTV has reached out to the Florida Department of Financial Services in Tallahassee to inquire about Bendel's case and the current status of her grant application.

cards.headline: Former Haitian national team players run soccer clinic for youth in Boca Raton
cards.teaser: L'Union Fait La Force Training Center hosted a clinic from June 25-28 teaching top-level Haitian soccer players, led by former Haiti national team captain and Atlantic High School graduate Jean-Marc Alexandre.
cards.body:
Former members of the Haitian national soccer team mentored young players in Boca Raton this week, just days after a match against Morocco. L'Union Fait La Force, a premier soccer development program run by former Haitian National Team members, is hosting a clinic from June 25-28. The program is led by former team captain Jean-Marc Alexandre, an Atlantic High School and Lynn University graduate who was a member of Real Salt Lake's 2009 MLS Cup-winning team. "The whole purpose of this camp is to give these kids a pathway to the youth national team, being that they're not living in Haiti, so we give opportunities to the next generation," Alexandre said.

Nohe Chevry, one of the young players participating, moved to Palm Beach County in 2022 from Haiti with his family due to unrest in the country. Finding a local soccer team became a top priority, leading him to the L'Union Fait La Force Training Center. "It's a great opportunity to learn; they've been through all of the soccer stuff, pro contracts, so they can teach us, and it's really kind of them to do that," Chevry said. Luis Etienne is also participating in the clinic. Chevry's ambitions extend beyond the week's training. "I will take this to a high level, and my goal is to play in the World Cup and probably win it," he said.

cards.headline: Lucky Shuck in Jupiter featured in Where's Walter segment
cards.teaser: The Lucky Shuck in Jupiter was revealed as the location for the first Where's Walter adventure, showcasing the waterfront restaurant founded by a professional athlete.
cards.body:
The Lucky Shuck in Jupiter was featured in a Where's Walter segment after clues revealed the restaurant could be reached by car or boat and was founded by a professional athlete. Chef John, who has worked there since the restaurant's inception, guided the segment through their oyster selection. The restaurant serves about five different types of oysters daily, with their house specialty being Jemma's Pearls, named in honor of Joe Namath's granddaughter and given to the football legend for his birthday.

The Lucky Shuck goes through approximately 40 cases of oysters per week, with each case containing roughly 100 oysters, totaling 4,000 oysters weekly. WPTV Shining a Light reporter TA Walker participated in the segment and shared that the restaurant holds personal significance for him, as it was the location of his first date with his now-husband, Charlie. The waterfront location allows diners to arrive by boat and enjoy fresh seafood while watching vessels pass by on Jupiter's waterways.

Eve Samples, executive director of Friends of the Everglades, called the facility a misuse of public funds, describing it as an obscene waste of about a billion taxpayer dollars. A recent proposal from Miami-Dade County's mayor would transfer the roughly 25,000-acre space to the National Park Service for conservation. However, Osceola said she does not trust government agencies to protect the land and believes the Miccosukee people are its rightful stewards. WPTV asked ICE about plans to protect the Everglades as they move out. ICE referred the inquiry to Florida's Division of Emergency Management, the agency leading restoration efforts.

cards.headline: Alligator Alcatraz detainees scattered across U.S. after facility closure
cards.teaser: Immigration attorney Richard Hujber says detainees from the now-closed Alligator Alcatraz have been sent to facilities in Louisiana, Texas, New Mexico and as far as Tacoma, Washington, creating challenges for legal battles.
cards.body:
Following the closure of Alligator Alcatraz, the controversial detention facility in the Florida Everglades, detainees have been scattered to facilities across the country. Immigration attorney Richard Hujber said detainees have been sent to Louisiana, Texas, New Mexico, and as far as Tacoma, Washington. According to Gov. Ron DeSantis, roughly 21,000 people have been deported from the facility since it opened nearly a year ago.

Hujber said the dispersal creates significant legal challenges because different circuit courts in different parts of the country have varying laws on bonds and immigration cases. With bond now out of reach for some detainees, Hujber said they face difficult decisions about whether to continue fighting for residency or asylum or self-deport. Anna Maria Hernandez's cousin was released just before the facility closed and is now under an order of supervision, allowing him to drive, work and live in the U.S. The Baker County facility in North Florida remains operational.

hero.headline: Fort Pierce's Florida Highwaymen Museum featured in America 250 Road Trip
hero.teaser: The Florida Highwaymen Museum in Fort Pierce is a featured stop on the America 250 Road Trip celebrating the nation's 250th birthday.
hero.body:
The city of Fort Pierce announced this week that the Florida Highwaymen Museum is part of the festivities celebrating the country's 250th birthday. The museum opened this year and celebrates 26 Black artists who began painting in the 1950s, creating bold, colorful landscapes of Florida's untouched beauty and selling them along the roadside when segregation kept them out of traditional galleries.

Located at 1234 Avenue D, the museum is the nation's only one with exhibitions that include paintings from each of the 26 renowned Highwaymen artists. Summer hours run from June 16 through July 31, with the museum open Saturday and Sunday from noon to 4 p.m.

The museum will be closed in August and reopen in September, featuring a new exhibit. Fall and spring hours from September 1 through June 15 will be expanded.

cards.headline: Former Haitian national team players mentor youth soccer players in Boca Raton clinic
cards.teaser: Former members of the Haitian national soccer team spent time in Boca Raton this week mentoring the next generation of players, just days after a Wednesday nigh.
cards.body:
Former members of the Haitian national soccer team mentored the next generation of players in Boca Raton this week, just days after a match against Morocco. The L'Union Fait La Force Training Center, a premier soccer development program run by former Haitian National Team members, is hosting a clinic from June 25 through 28. Jean-Marc Alexandre, former Haiti national team captain and member of Real Salt Lake's 2009 MLS Cup-winning team, leads the program. Alexandre is an Atlantic High School and Lynn University graduate.

For participants like Nohe Chevry and Luis Etienne, the clinic provides instruction on the sport and potential exposure to the national team. Chevry moved to Palm Beach County with his family in 2022 as unrest grew in Haiti, and finding a local soccer team became a top priority. "The whole purpose of this camp is to give these kids a pathway to the youth national team, being that they're not living in Haiti, so we give opportunities to the next generation," Alexandre said. Chevry said his goal is to play in the World Cup and win it.

cards.headline: Vero Beach group collects donations for Venezuela earthquake victims through Saturday
cards.teaser: Latinas Nexus Network in Vero Beach is hosting a Venezuela Earthquake Relief Drive, collecting essential supplies through Saturday for communities devastated by a massive earthquake.
cards.body:
Latinas Nexus Network in Vero Beach is hosting a Venezuela Earthquake Relief Drive to collect essential supplies for communities devastated by a 7.5 magnitude earthquake. The drive is being organized by founders Lourana Navarro and Juliana Marino, along with Heidi Ramirez. Navarro, who was born in Venezuela and now lives in Vero Beach, said her family in Caracas is safe, but surrounding communities have lost everything. She expressed concern about the scale of destruction, noting that recovery will take decades and that the country lacks sufficient resources. The organizers are working with Global Empowerment Mission to ship collected supplies to Venezuela, ensuring 100% of donations go directly through verified humanitarian relief efforts.

Needed items include powder Gatorade, non-perishable food, baby formula, diapers, feminine hygiene products, first aid kits, blankets, sleeping bags, flashlights, batteries, soap, shampoo, toothbrushes, toothpaste, toilet paper, cleaning supplies, hand sanitizer, face masks, nitrile gloves, plastic bins with lids, and heavy duty garbage bags. Donations can be dropped off at 684 Old Dixie Hwy, Vero Beach through Saturday, June 27, 2026, from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. For more information, contact Lourana Navarro at 954-205-0700, Juliana Marino at 772-913-0805, or Heidi Ramirez at 772-213-2747.

cards.headline: SoFlo Market brings patriotic family fun to Boca Raton City Hall on July 4
cards.teaser: The popular SoFlo Market will turn Boca Raton City Hall into a hub of red, white and blue celebration on Independence Day with free family entertainment and local vendors.
cards.body:
Founder and organizer Tatiana Freitas is bringing a patriotic celebration to Boca Raton City Hall on Saturday, July 4. The free monthly SoFlo Market will draw families, food lovers and local shopping enthusiasts from across Palm Beach County with extra Independence Day flair including a kids' parade, DJ, unique vendors and gourmet food. The first 20 children through the gate will receive a free gift.

The event runs from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. at Boca Raton City Hall, 201 West Palmetto Park Road, and offers face painting, a foggy bubble station, mini golf, balloon twisting, handmade crafts and desserts. A live appearance by the SoFlo Market's flamingo mascot is planned as a crowd favorite. Boca Raton firefighters and police officers have been invited to share the day with residents. Kyle, Freitas' son, and Eddie, her husband, are part of the organizing team. Admission is free.

cards.headline: West Boca Raton homeowner faces new hurdles with My Safe Florida Home grant despite completed work
cards.teaser: Anne Bendel says her efforts to receive a promised grant from the state to fix up her home keep facing one hurdle after another, despite completing all required work.
cards.body:
Anne Bendel, a West Boca Raton homeowner, has encountered repeated obstacles in her attempt to receive a My Safe Florida Home grant despite completing all required work on her home. Bendel first contacted WPTV in May regarding a delay caused by paperwork from her insurance company, an issue that was eventually resolved. My Safe Florida Home then informed her in May that her status was complete. However, a week later, representatives asked for additional documentation, including a permit of completion for a large impact window. After Bendel provided the permit, the agency raised questions about dates on the paperwork. Her application is now back under review, leaving her uncertain about receiving any grant funding toward the $8,000 she paid out of pocket.

The My Safe Florida Home program offers grants of up to $10,000 to homeowners across Florida to fortify homes against storms and earn insurance discounts. The program has helped thousands of residents. WPTV has contacted the Florida Department of Financial Services in Tallahassee regarding Bendel's case and the status of her grant. Bendel expressed frustration with the process, stating that she completed all required work, obtained permits, and secured the insurance the program requested, yet continues to face additional requests from the agency.

cards.headline: Alligator Alcatraz detainees scattered across U.S. as legal battles continue after closure
cards.teaser: After Alligator Alcatraz shut down, detainees have been sent to facilities in Louisiana, Texas, New Mexico and as far as Tacoma, Washington, creating massive challenges for families and attorneys.
cards.body:
Immigration attorney Richard Hujber said detainees from the closed Alligator Alcatraz facility have been scattered across the country to detention centers in Louisiana, Texas, New Mexico, and as far as Tacoma, Washington. This dispersal creates significant legal challenges because immigration law varies across different circuit courts in different regions of the country, with some circuits denying bonds that might be approved elsewhere. For detainees unable to secure bond, the situation has become dire, leaving them to question whether continuing to fight for residency or asylum is worthwhile or if self-deportation is their only option.

Gov. Ron DeSantis reported that roughly 21,000 people have been deported from the facility since it opened nearly a year ago. Some families experienced bittersweet outcomes following the closure. Anna Maria Hernandez's cousin was released just before Alligator Alcatraz shut down and is now under an order of supervision, which allows him to drive, work and live in the U.S. The Baker County facility in North Florida remains operational. For many former detainees and their families, however, the future remains uncertain as legal battles continue.

hero.headline: SoFlo Market brings July 4 celebration with kids parade, free gifts to Boca Raton City Hall
hero.teaser: The popular monthly market will turn Boca Raton City Hall into a hub of red, white and blue celebration this Independence Day with free admission, local vendors, and patriotic activities.
hero.body:
The popular SoFlo Market is gearing up to turn Boca Raton City Hall into a hub of red, white and blue celebration this Independence Day, says founder and organizer Tatiana Freitas. The free monthly event will take place Saturday, July 4, drawing families, food lovers and local shopping enthusiasts from across Palm Beach County. Freitas told WPTV the market's mission is to uplift small local businesses and bring the community together. For the holiday, organizers are adding extra patriotic flair, including a kids parade, a DJ, unique vendors, gourmet food and the first 20 children through the gate receiving a free gift.

Visitors can expect face painting, a foggy bubble station, mini golf, and balloon twisting, alongside the market's signature array of handmade crafts and mouthwatering desserts. A live appearance by the SoFlo Market's flamboyant flamingo mascot is set to be a crowd favorite. Boca Raton firefighters and police officers have been invited to share the day with residents, reinforcing the family-first atmosphere.

Kyle, Freitas' son, and Eddie, her husband, are part of the organizing team ensuring activities run smoothly. Electricity will be powered by generators on-site. The SoFlo Market runs monthly, but Freitas says the Independence Day edition is always a standout. The event runs from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. at Boca Raton City Hall, 201 West Palmetto Park Road.

cards.headline: Florida Mango Festival showcases 75 vendors, rare varieties at West Palm Beach Convention Center today
cards.teaser: Florida-grown mangoes will take center stage Saturday, June 27, at the Florida Mango Festival inside the Palm Beach County Convention Center.
cards.body:
Florida-grown mangoes will take center stage Saturday, June 27, at the Florida Mango Festival inside the Palm Beach County Convention Center. Organizers said the event will feature more than 75 vendors serving up local mango varieties, grafted trees, tropical fruits, and mango-themed products. Alex Salazar of Tropical Acres Farms told WPTV's T.A. Walker that the indoor, air-conditioned venue offers an ideal setting for people to taste, learn, and discover the magic of Florida-grown mangoes without worrying about the summer heat.

Festival co-organizer Vince Rogers previewed some of the state's most unique varieties, including Fruit Cocktail with its sweet, multi-layered flavor; Orange Sherbet, offering creamy citrus notes; and Pineapple Pleasure with tropical pineapple undertones. He noted Florida hosts more than 350 mango varieties, far beyond what's typically available in grocery stores. Throughout the day, visitors can attend educational talks on home mango growing and grafting techniques, with Salazar leading demonstrations. Additional features include an ID Your Mango booth, a scion exchange for online mango community members, and a master display of Florida's diverse mango cultivars. The festival runs from 10:30 a.m. at 650 Okeechobee Blvd., West Palm Beach. First pick ticket holders can enter at 9 a.m. Garage parking is included with admission. Tickets and more information are available at floridamangofestival.com.

cards.headline: Peggy Adams Animal Rescue League urges South Florida pet owners to create hurricane disaster plans
cards.teaser: The organization recommends microchipping, emergency kits, and hurricane drills as Florida's hurricane season runs through November.
cards.body:
With hurricane season in full swing, Peggy Adams Animal Rescue League is urging South Florida residents to create a disaster plan for their pets before the next storm hits. Dr. Alyssa Comroe, CEO of Peggy Adams, told WPTV the safest place for pets during a hurricane is right alongside their owners.

The shelter's expert team recommends several key steps for pet safety. Pet owners should ensure pets wear a collar with current identification and have an updated microchip registered with correct contact information. Residents should introduce pets to a designated safe room ahead of time, such as a walk-in closet or downstairs bathroom, and conduct practice runs so the hurricane isn't their first time there. Pet owners should prepare an emergency kit with a three-day supply of food and water in airtight containers, bowls, a sturdy carrier, bedding, towels, medications for two weeks, vaccination records, first-aid supplies, litter and box for cats, leashes, harnesses, cool packs, wipes, waste bags, and multiple forms of visible ID. Additional recommendations include keeping a printed list of local pet-friendly shelters and hotels in an accessible place, keeping recent photos of pets with their owner to help with identification if separated, and conducting hurricane drills that include pets' daily routines inside the safe room to maximize comfort later. Florida's hurricane season runs June through November.

cards.headline: Boca Raton's George Snow Scholarship Fund awards record $7.5 million to 470 students across Palm Beach, Broward counties
cards.teaser: The nonprofit, the largest scholarship provider in Palm Beach County, has now distributed more than $45 million to over 4,100 students since its founding over 40 years ago.
cards.body:
The George Snow Scholarship Fund, headquartered in Boca Raton, has announced a record-breaking 2026, awarding more than $7.5 million in scholarships and support services to 470 students across Palm Beach and Broward counties. Founded over 40 years ago, the nonprofit has now distributed more than $45 million to over 4,100 students, making it the largest scholarship provider in Palm Beach County. According to President Tim Snow, the program bridges the gap between traditional financial aid and what students and families can afford by offering four-year scholarship commitments that provide stability throughout college. Vice President of Development Jay Brandt noted that GSSF's services extend beyond financial assistance, including mentorship, professional development, and resources like the College Compass podcast.

Zya Chow, a Wellington Community High School graduate and 2026 recipient, earned both the Royal Palm Hearing Aid Scholarship and the Davidowitz Family Caregiving Youth Scholarship and plans to attend Georgetown University. The fund also operates the Doyle-Whelchel Scholars Boutique, led by Scholar Services Coordinator Garvey Antoine, which provides professional, formal, and casual clothing to help scholars prepare for interviews, internships, and campus life. The boutique accepts donations of new or gently used clothing, footwear, and accessories from the community.

hero.headline: Florida farm labor cases mirror Italy's migrant worker exploitation system
hero.body:
Federal prosecutors in Tampa and across Florida have brought forced labor cases against farm contractors that operate using methods similar to criminal systems documented in Italy. The Italian case involved four migrant workers who were burned alive in a van in Calabria after demanding unpaid wages. Experts describe this type of exploitation as the gangmaster economy, where criminal intermediaries control workers through debt, threats and isolation. In Italy, this system has a specific name: caporalato. The caporale recruits workers, controls transportation, decides pay rates and determines where workers sleep and whether they can leave.

The Italian system has adapted to changing migration patterns. For decades, caporalato was associated with traditional Italian organized crime groups. But a division of labor has emerged where foreign criminal networks now handle direct control of workers because they better understand migrant vulnerabilities. Many workers now come from Afghanistan, Pakistan, Syria and other distant countries. These workers often arrive with travel debts, do not speak Italian, lack local connections and depend entirely on intermediaries for work, transportation and housing. Criminal networks exploit this dependence, even threatening relatives in workers' home countries to enforce compliance.

In Florida, Alexander Villatoro Moreno, known as Quichi, was sentenced to 70 months in prison on June 9 in federal court in Tampa after pleading guilty to a RICO conspiracy. He and co-defendants operated Los Villatoros Harvesting, which brought Mexican workers to the United States on H-2A agricultural visas. Prosecutors said workers were promised fair wages and good conditions but faced excessive recruitment fees and debt upon arrival. They were kept in crowded housing, isolated from outsiders, verbally humiliated and threatened with arrest or deportation. The conspirators also threatened to harm workers' family members in Mexico. A second case involved Martha Zeferino Jose, her partner and her son, charged in a 35-count indictment in February involving Las Princesas Corp. According to prosecutors, the company recruited Mexican H-2A workers for farms and nurseries in Virginia, North Carolina and Florida while confiscating documents, imposing debts, providing degrading housing and threatening deportation.

The H-2A program is a legal guest worker system that many employers use lawfully. However, a worker arriving with papers remains vulnerable. They may depend on a single employer for their job, one contractor for transportation and one document for their legal status. If that chain turns criminal, the legal route becomes part of the trap. Federal prosecutors have used forced labor and racketeering laws against farm contractors, but convictions often come years after workers have suffered. By that time, the system has already inflicted damage. Italy announced increased farm inspections after the Calabria killings, but the question of timing remains difficult.

cards.headline: DeSantis signs stablecoin regulation and virtual currency kiosk safety bills
cards.teaser: Florida will regulate stablecoins under federal standards and require fraud warnings on cryptocurrency kiosks starting in October.
cards.body:
Ron DeSantis signed three bills Friday that directly impact Florida's financial services and treatment of money. CS/CS/HB 175 brings regulation for stablecoins in accordance with federal law and goes into effect in October. The Office of Financial Regulation will determine whether an entity qualifies as a "qualified payment stablecoin issuer," either with a money services business license or by granting a certificate of approval to trust companies. Stablecoins can be used for financial settlement under the law, with value fixed at a rate of exchange with the U.S. dollar.

CS/CS/SB 1568 establishes the Florida Stablecoin Pilot Program within the Department of Financial Services. Applicants and licensees who interact with DFS can voluntarily pay certain licensing, registration, application and renewal fees using approved payment stablecoins. The department will determine which stablecoins qualify based on strict financial safeguards, such as being fully backed by reserve assets valued at least $1 billion. HB 505 requires virtual currency kiosk operators to register with OFR and display a fraud warning on initial screens. Transaction limits are capped at $2,000 a day for new users and $10,000 a day for established customers. Legislators hope the bill may stop people from being scammed into using these devices under duress or ignorance.

cards.headline: DeSantis vetoes inmate commercial driver training and naturopathic medicine board
cards.teaser: The governor rejected bills to train nonviolent inmates as truck drivers and create a naturopathic medicine licensing board.
cards.body:
Ron DeSantis vetoed two pieces of legislation Friday night. HB 325 would have expanded training for commercial drivers licenses to nonviolent inmates with two years or less remaining on their sentences, expanding eligibility already available to work-release inmates. While it passed unanimously in the Senate and House, DeSantis said legislators missed unintended consequences and deemed the program unnecessarily burdensome to the Department of Corrections. He cited significant public safety concerns regarding inmate driver training. Legislators believed the bill would not impose new impacts or costs on the prison system. According to the House bill analysis, the shortage of commercial truck drivers in this country is estimated at 80,000 currently but is expected to rise with an anticipated need to replace 1.2 million retiring drivers. The lack of American citizens willing to drive trucks has led to foreign-born drivers behind the wheel.

DeSantis also vetoed SB/CS 688, which would have created the Board of Naturopathic Medicine within the Department of Health and set guidelines for practitioners. He said doctors and dietitians can already prescribe or recommend naturopathic remedies and that the bill could impact current practitioners by imposing new bureaucratic hurdles, including post-graduate education not available in the state. DeSantis previously vetoed bills tracking e-bike and scooter crashes and making it easier for high school students to volunteer as poll workers. More vetoes are expected regarding budget line items before he signs the budget Monday, ahead of the July 1 fiscal year start.

cards.headline: Florida pavilion opens at Great American State Fair on National Mall
cards.teaser: The state showcases its history, agriculture, wildlife and tourism at the exposition celebrating America's 250th anniversary in Washington, D.C.
cards.body:
The Florida Pavilion opened Thursday at the Great American State Fair in Washington, D.C., joining exhibits from every state and six U.S. territories at the expo hosted by Freedom 250 on the National Mall through July 10. The exhibit highlights the people, places, industries from space to agriculture, and culture that make Florida a destination. Gov. Ron DeSantis said in a statement that Florida is proud to showcase the culture and history that has helped shape America, noting the state's natural beauty, agriculture, and world-class attractions.

Visitors begin their journey in St. Augustine, the nation's oldest continuously inhabited European-established city, where Florida's story begins with Juan Ponce de León's arrival in 1513. The pavilion features five signature experiences: Florida's History Heritage, The Manatee: Florida's Iconic Marine Mammal, Florida's Natural Resources, Fresh From Florida: Florida's Agricultural Heritage, and Live More Floridays, a celebration of Florida tourism. The Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission participates with an interactive exhibit showcasing Florida's iconic wildlife, world-renowned fisheries, and natural landscapes. FWC Executive Director Roger Young said visitors will discover why Florida is recognized as the Fishing and Boating Capital of the World. The fair is open Sunday through Wednesday from 10 a.m. and Thursday through Saturday from 10 a.m. to 11 p.m., with extended hours until midnight on July 4.

cards.headline: Byron Donalds adds $688,000 to gubernatorial campaign in single week
cards.teaser: The congressman continues to dominate fundraising in the Republican primary with nearly $66 million on hand.
cards.body:
Byron Donalds extended his fundraising dominance in the Republican gubernatorial primary with nearly $253,000 added to his campaign account and another $435,000 to the Friends of Byron Donalds PAC in the week ending June 19. Donalds now has nearly $66 million on hand, though that total will decrease following a $20 million media buy he has booked. Despite the planned spending, he continues to significantly outpace his three main rivals in fundraising strength.

James Fishback raised $4,825 to his campaign account and nothing to his Florida First PAC, leaving him with roughly $117,000 total to spend as of June 19. Jay Collins raised just over $11,000 to his campaign account and $1,500 to his political committee during the same week, with approximately $3.5 million remaining to spend. Former House Speaker Paul Renner raised less than $30,000 to his campaign account for the second straight fundraising period and $13,000 to his PAC, with roughly $2.5 million available as of June 19. No candidates will debate at Saturday's Florida GOP event, with Donalds and his allies arguing his opponents are not viable.

cards.headline: Attorney General Uthmeier raises $1 million in latest weekly report
cards.teaser: The Republican incumbent stretches his cash lead over Democratic challenger Jose Javier Rodriguez ahead of the November election.
cards.body:
Attorney General James Uthmeier reported raising $1.009 million to his Friends of James Uthmeier political committee and an additional $5,054 to his campaign account in the week ending June 19. A $900,000 check from the Republican Party of Florida made up the majority of the contribution. Other notable donors included The Southern Group and political consultant Alex Bruesewitz. Uthmeier has accumulated more than $8 million in his political committee and nearly $1.1 million in his campaign account ahead of the November election.

Democratic challenger Jose Javier Rodriguez, a former state senator from South Florida, brought in $13,231 during the same period, marking his weakest filing to date, though it represents the first weekly report of the 2026 cycle. Rodriguez had roughly $215,000 on hand as of June 19. The financial disparity underscores Uthmeier's substantial resource advantage as the race heads into the fall.

cards.headline: Agriculture Commissioner Simpson donates $3 million to Senate campaigns
cards.teaser: Wilton Simpson raised nearly $450,000 for his re-election in one week but contributed $3 million to the Florida Republican Senatorial Campaign Committee.
cards.body:
Trilby egg farmer Wilton Simpson, Florida's agriculture commissioner, continued his dominant fundraising effort in the week ending June 19, raising $449,400 between his campaign account and the Friends of Wilton Simpson political committee. However, the week was marked more by his significant donation than his intake. Simpson gave $3 million to the Florida Republican Senatorial Campaign Committee, which supports statewide efforts for the state Senate that Simpson once led. Despite the major contribution, Simpson maintains roughly $31 million across his various political accounts, including his campaign account, the Friends of Wilton Simpson committee, the Florida Green PAC, Future Florida and the Home Grown PAC.

Simpson's opponents are not approaching his financial position. Primary challenger Matt Taylor raised just over $6,000 during the week and has less than $69,000 on hand. Democrats Joey Mendoza Atkins and Don Prichard raised no money during the week, with Prichard carrying roughly $7,000 and Atkins holding less than $100. Write-in candidate Kyle Gibson has struggled to file fundraising reports, making his available funds unclear, with the Division of Elections already issuing him multiple letters for failing to report his numbers.

hero.headline: William 'Bill' Hauserman dies in Palm City
hero.teaser: William 'Bill' Hauserman of Palm City has died, according to Forest Hills Memorial Park & Palm City Chapel.
hero.body:
William 'Bill' Hauserman of Palm City has died, according to an obituary posted by Forest Hills Memorial Park & Palm City Chapel. The obituary was published Friday evening.

No additional details about Hauserman's life or memorial services were included in the brief notice.

The 10-Cent Bridge connects the mainland to Hutchinson Island. No details about the circumstances of the crash or the identity of the defendant were included in the brief report.

hero.teaser: The Florida Department of Environmental Protection issued fines to Fort Pierce over unpermitted docks at a local establishment.
hero.body:
The Florida Department of Environmental Protection has fined the city of Fort Pierce for unpermitted docks at an iconic bar in the area. The fines were issued for docking structures that were constructed without proper environmental permits.

The enforcement action targets violations related to waterfront development regulations. The specific bar and exact fine amounts were not detailed in available reports.

cards.headline: Missing diver found dead on ocean floor near Fort Pierce Inlet
cards.teaser: A missing diver was found dead on the ocean floor approximately 6 to 7 miles north-northeast of the Fort Pierce Inlet on Friday afternoon.
cards.body:
The St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office is investigating after a missing diver was found dead on the ocean floor approximately 6 to 7 miles north-northeast of the Fort Pierce Inlet. The U.S. Coast Guard Station Fort Pierce received a Mayday call over VHF Channel 16 at approximately 11:30 a.m. Friday regarding the missing diver. Following the distress call, the Coast Guard notified the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission, which immediately deployed 4 vessels to assist in the search. The St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office Marine Unit, which had independently monitored the Mayday call, was already en route to assist. A group of civilian boaters who were friends of the missing diver departed the Fort Pierce Inlet at approximately 1 p.m., and aerial support was provided by both the Coast Guard and FWC.

Responding units made contact with the vessel involved nearly due east of Avalon State Park. At approximately 4:10 p.m., civilian divers entered the water and located the missing diver at the bottom of the ocean in approximately 55 feet of water. The diver was recovered and pronounced deceased. The deceased was transported to Coast Guard Station Fort Pierce. The St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office Criminal Investigations Division is conducting the investigation into the circumstances surrounding the incident, which remains ongoing.

cards.headline: Major crash blocks two right lanes on I-95 north in St. Lucie County
cards.teaser: A major crash blocked two right lanes on Interstate 95 northbound in St. Lucie County on Friday evening.
cards.body:
Two right lanes on I-95 north in St. Lucie County were blocked Friday evening due to a major crash, according to Florida 511. The incident caused traffic delays on the northbound side of the interstate.

Florida 511 reported the lane blockages as motorists were advised of the crash.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie toy gun incident leads to armed confrontation
cards.teaser: An incident involving a toy gun in Port St. Lucie escalated to an armed confrontation, prompting police response.
cards.body:
A toy gun incident in Port St. Lucie led to an armed confrontation that drew law enforcement response. The incident underscores concerns about realistic-looking toy weapons and their potential to trigger dangerous situations.

Authorities are emphasizing the need for young people to understand how their actions with replica weapons can be perceived by others and law enforcement. The specific location and individuals involved were not identified in the initial reports.

cards.headline: 15-year-old St. Lucie County girl missing for 3 weeks
cards.teaser: St. Lucie County deputies are seeking tips to locate a 15-year-old girl who has been missing for three weeks.
cards.body:
A 15-year-old girl from St. Lucie County has been missing for three weeks, and deputies are asking the public for information. The St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office is seeking any tips that could help locate the missing teenager.

Deputies are working to determine the girl's whereabouts and ensure her safety. Anyone with information about her location is being asked to contact the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office.

cards.teaser: A sailing yacht valued at $16 million sank in Fort Pierce waters.
cards.body: The sailing yacht Legacy, worth $16 million, sank in Fort Pierce. The vessel went down in local waters, marking a significant maritime incident for the area. The incident is under investigation by maritime authorities.

cards.headline: Six favorite restaurants in Port St. Lucie and Fort Pierce highlighted
cards.teaser: A list of six popular restaurants in Port St. Lucie and Fort Pierce has been compiled for local diners.
cards.body:
Six restaurants in Port St. Lucie and Fort Pierce have been featured as local favorites. The dining establishments represent popular choices for residents and visitors across the two St. Lucie County cities.

The restaurants span various cuisines and dining experiences available in the area. The list offers residents options for dining out in their local communities.

hero.headline: Vero Beach group collects donations for Venezuela earthquake victims through Saturday
hero.body:
A Vero Beach organization is collecting donations for communities devastated by a massive earthquake in Venezuela, with organizers emphasizing the urgent need for assistance. Latinas Nexus Network is hosting a Venezuela Earthquake Relief Drive to gather essential supplies that will be shipped directly to affected areas. The initiative is being led by founders Lourana Navarro and Juliana Marino, along with Heidi Ramirez.

Navarro, who was born in Venezuela and now lives in Vero Beach, said her own family in Caracas is safe, but surrounding communities have suffered tremendous losses. "When I started seeing the magnitude and that it was a 7.5, I really got scared," Navarro said. She emphasized that the scale of destruction extends far beyond immediate relief needs. "Seeing the devastation, I know this is going to take decades to recover. We as a country don't have the resources," she said. Marino stressed the organization's commitment to directing help where it matters most. "From here, the only thing that I can do is do our best to come together and help them and find different resources so we can get it directly to the people and bring the help that they need," Marino said.

The organizers are partnering with Global Empowerment Mission to ensure supplies reach Venezuela, with a commitment that 100 percent of donations will go through verified humanitarian relief efforts. Marino noted the massive scope of the crisis, stating "We're talking, hundreds of thousands of people that are in need right now." According to Navarro, the most critical shortages are food and shelter. "I can tell you that the worst is the food and the place to sleep, to take a bath, they don't have that right now," Navarro said. The group is collecting powder Gatorade, non-perishable food, baby formula and baby food, diapers in all sizes, baby wipes, feminine hygiene products, soap, shampoo, toothbrushes and toothpaste, rain boots, toilet paper, blankets, sleeping bags, flashlights and batteries, heavy duty garbage bags, first aid kits, bandages and gauze, hand sanitizer, cleaning supplies, face masks, nitrile gloves, and plastic bins with lids.

Donations can be dropped off at 684 Old Dixie Hwy in Vero Beach through Saturday, June 27, 2026, between 9 a.m. and 5 p.m. The founders emphasized that the relief drive welcomes support from everyone in the community. "We are asking not just the Hispanic community, we are asking everyone. They really need us," they said. For more information, contact Lourana Navarro at (954) 205-0700, Juliana Marino at (772) 913-0805, or Heidi Ramirez at (772) 213-2747.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce Florida Highwaymen Museum featured in America 250 Road Trip celebration
cards.teaser: The Florida Highwaymen Museum in Fort Pierce, which opened this year, is a featured stop on the America 250 Road Trip celebrating the nation's 250th birthday.
cards.body:
The Florida Highwaymen Museum, which opened this year in Fort Pierce, has been announced as a featured stop on the America 250 Road Trip. The city made the announcement on its Facebook page this week as part of celebrations for the country's 250th birthday. The museum celebrates 26 Black artists who began painting in the 1950s, creating bold, colorful landscapes of Florida's untouched beauty and selling them along the roadside when segregation kept them out of traditional galleries.

Located at 1234 Avenue D, the museum is the nation's only one with exhibitions that include paintings from each of the 26 renowned Highwaymen artists. Through July 31, the museum is open Saturdays and Sundays from noon to 4 p.m. The museum will be closed in August and reopen in September with a new exhibit. Fall and spring hours from September 1 through June 15 will be expanded.
